Ransomware Attack Disrupts Operations Across Egypt’s Fisheries Sector

A sophisticated ransomware attack has struck Egypt’s fisheries industry, disrupting IT systems at multiple firms and severely affecting daily operations at fish processing plants, hatcheries, and aquaculture sites across the Nile Delta and Red Sea regions. The incident, first detected early Monday morning, has left production lines halted, site operations suspended, and workers uncertain about when normal activities will resume.

According to the Egyptian Fisheries Industry Association (EFIA), at least six companies, including NileCatch Foods, AquaHarvest Group, and RedSea Aquafarms, have reported locked computer systems and inaccessible production data, with ransom demands delivered in encrypted messages. Industry officials say that the attack has crippled scheduling, inventory management, and quality control functions, forcing plant managers to send workers home or reassign them to manual tasks where possible.

“We’re facing a total shutdown of our digital infrastructure,” said Mahmoud El-Sharif, operations manager at NileCatch Foods. “Our processing plant in Damietta has not been able to track incoming or outgoing shipments, and our automated grading systems are offline, so we can’t maintain output or guarantee quality.”

The ransomware has prevented several sites from accessing feeding schedules and environmental monitoring data for their aquaculture facilities, raising concerns about the welfare of fish stocks. “Staff are doing their best to monitor conditions manually, but without our integrated monitoring system, there’s a risk to both stock health and yields,” explained Laila Fathy, technical director at AquaHarvest Group.

Workers across affected firms have reported confusion and anxiety. “We don’t know if we’ll be paid this week,” said Hassan Ali, a supervisor at RedSea Aquafarms. “With the systems down, payroll and attendance are being processed by hand, and many of us have been told to stay home until further notice.”

The EFIA has urged members to refrain from interacting with the attackers and to work with cybersecurity experts and law enforcement. “We are coordinating with national authorities and industry stakeholders to assess the full extent of the attack and support affected firms,” said EFIA Secretary-General Dr. Nourhan Ghoneim. “Our immediate priority is restoring operations and safeguarding our workers’ livelihoods.”

Industry analysts estimate that with over 40,000 workers employed in Egypt’s fisheries sector, the potential daily production losses could exceed EGP 30 million. As the attack continues, the EFIA warns that prolonged downtime could threaten supply continuity and the financial stability of smaller firms.

At press time, efforts to restore affected systems were ongoing, with no timeline yet for full recovery.
